bill.title: A joint resolution terminating the national emergency declared to impose duties on articles imported from Canada.
subjects: Presidents and presidential powers, Vice Presidents
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution terminates the national emergency declared by President Donald J. Trump on February 1, 2025, which imposed an additional 25% tariff on most imports from Canada (except for Canadian energy or energy resources, which have an additional 10% tariff).

classification.plainSummary: This resolution would end the national emergency that President Trump declared on February 1, 2025, which imposed a 25% tariff on most goods imported from Canada and a 10% tariff on Canadian energy imports. Terminating the emergency would remove the legal basis for these additional duties on Canadian products.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly affects the 10% tariff on Canadian energy and energy resources.
The 25% tariff on most Canadian imports affects manufacturers who source materials, components, or finished goods from Canada.
Retailers importing consumer goods from Canada face the 25% tariff that this resolution would eliminate.
Agricultural products and food imports from Canada are subject to the 25% tariff.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would end the national emergency declared by President Donald J. Trump on February 1, 2025, which imposed an additional 25% tariff on most imports from Canada (except for Canadian energy or energy resources, which have an additional 10% tariff).
plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who buys imported goods, and people who make goods here.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in prices, and what is made where. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
